verdicts.why: Vigour and freshness are what the word means in this sense, not an attitude laid over it; a young face is a description, and approval, where it comes, comes from valuing youth rather than from the word.
A young company or a night that is young is placed on a timeline and nothing more; no plain neighbour is being passed over to signal how the speaker feels.
A sequencing connector; it orders events and takes no side on any of them.
Marks a consequence or inference ('not so undeserving, then') and carries no attitude toward what it connects.
Points at a time and nothing else; there is no judgement to be had in 'she then sat still'.
A grammatical comparative marker; whatever judgement is present lives in the adjective it modifies ('more wrong and reprehensible'), not in 'more'.
States a greater degree and no more; 'deaden them more' is measured, not evaluated, by the word.
The affection and trust are the relationship being named, not the speaker's attitude added on top; 'his friend' describes who someone is to someone, the way 'sister' does.
In the loose 'acquaintance' sense ('a large party of friends') it is a plain count of people one knows, with no warmth or coolness in the choice of word.
Names a role of cooperation or support (a friend of the cause, a friend at court) without praising or disparaging the person who fills it.
A quantifier over mass nouns ('much more difference'); it sizes, it does not judge.
A quantifier over count nouns ('two or three more of the men'); pure number, no attitude.
Reports that an emotion is undergone ('felt any anger', 'felt persuaded') without the speaker taking a side on the feeling or the feeler; it is the plain verb of its field.
Saying one feels rather than thinks marks the grounds as intuitive, which is part of the meaning, not a judgement aimed at the belief or its holder.
Being conscious of a state ('she felt that years of happiness could not...') is described, not appraised; the verb is neutral against every neighbour.
The plain verb for using language; 'as he spoke' passes no judgement on the speaker or the speech.
To speak to or with someone names the exchange and takes no side on it; slightly more formal than 'talk' but not loaded.
Expressing something in speech ('I do not speak it to be thanked') is a plain report of the act, with no attitude carried by the verb.
A walled space in a building; the paradigm of a word that describes without judging, like 'table'.
Space for movement ('no room to turn') is a plain measure of available space, without approval or contempt.
'Room for improvement' or 'room for doubt' names an opening; any judgement lies in what fills the slot, not in 'room'.
A household living together is named, not judged; 'the Longbourn family' is a plain designation, and the disgrace in nearby sentences belongs to the events, not the word.
Parents and children as a social unit; the word is the plain term for the referent, with no warmer or cooler neighbour it is chosen against.
A line of descent ('the family of De Bourgh') is described genealogically; any prestige attached comes from the name that follows, not from 'family'.
The plain verb for letting something be known; 'she told me all about it' reports the act with no attitude toward teller, hearer or news.
